1:
Who the assembly and its gods are is the question the psalm opens with. Charles Ellicott renders it the assembly of God, or divine assembly, meaning Israel in its religious character, and notes that the verb has an official ring, being used elsewhere of departmental officers, so that the psalm begins by stating that God has taken his official place as president of the bench of judges; the gods are men delegated with office from him, and the custom of designating his vicegerents by the divine name was very natural, the whole point of a later verse lying in that double sense. John Wesley and Matthew Henry agree that magistrates are called gods because they have their commission from God and act as his deputies. John Gill keeps another option open, reporting that one version renders the assembly as the congregation of angels and that the Targum interprets it of the righteous. Keil and Delitzsch close that door by name: two critics have understood angels by the word and inscribed the psalm as God’s judgment upon unjust judges in heaven and on earth, but angels as such are nowhere so called in the Old Testament. Augustine of Hippo shuts it more broadly still, saying that far be it from us to understand here the gods of the Gentiles, or idols, or any creature in heaven or earth except men.

When the psalm was written is answered from one passage by two voices. Adam Clarke thinks it was probably composed when a king of Judah reformed the courts of justice throughout his states, since in instructing the judges he uses nearly the same words as the psalm’s opening. John Calvin reports that reading from a Jewish commentator and sets beside it another that puts the psalm in a later reign, in reference to certain wicked magistrates. Keil and Delitzsch defend the inscription instead: nothing militates against the psalm having been written by the Asaph who was David’s contemporary, except a determination not to allow the heading its most natural sense; and they find it perfectly characteristic of that writer to plunge into the contemplation of divine judgment and to introduce God as speaking. Augustine of Hippo reads the name itself, which he says signifies the Synagogue.

Adam Clarke illustrates the divine presence in court from English practice. The Court of King’s Bench, he observes, is properly the place where the king presides and where he is supposed always to be present, though the kings of England seldom appear there; one of them sometimes attended, and at such times it might be said that the king is in the king’s court. Judges, he concludes, should beware what they do, for God is in his court and in the midst of the assembly he will judge. C.H. Spurgeon puts the same warning nearer home, that village squires and country magistrates would do well to remember it, some of them needing to go to school to the psalmist; judges shall be judged, and even the judgments of our most impartial judges will be revised by a higher court. On the reproof itself Charles Ellicott hears a terrible severity in the divine how long, and quotes the lines in which the gods grow angry at men’s patience and justice is bidden rouse itself as crimes grow; he explains the accepting of persons from the eastern custom of prostration before a judge, the accepted suitor being told to lift up his face. Adam Clarke reads the same phrase as encouraging the wicked in their oppressions. John Gill makes the speaker the divine person standing in the assembly, calling the unjust judges to account for a long course of wrong judgment.
3:
On the duty laid on the judges John Gill defines the parties as those who have no money to carry on a suit and no friends to abide by them, and grounds the charge in the title: since they are called gods they ought to imitate him whose name they bear, who is the Father of the fatherless. Adam Clarke puts it as an office, that the judges are the natural protectors of the oppressed under God and must punish their oppressors however rich or powerful. Charles Ellicott corrects the vocabulary, rendering the first word as miserable rather than poor and noting that the two verses use different words.

Whether the ignorance of the fifth verse is a defect or a choice divides the entry. Adam Clarke makes it both: the judges are not acquainted with the law of God on which all their decisions should be founded, and they are ignorant and do not wish to be instructed — they will not learn, and they cannot teach. Charles Ellicott puts the weight on the will: the men are infatuated by their position and blinded by pride, and the clause about walking in darkness is better rendered that they let themselves walk in darkness, the conjugation implying that inclination and not circumstance brings this dullness to the dictates of justice. He adds that such moral blindness sometimes darkens those in whom intellectual light is keenest, and names a famous chancellor as the case. John Wesley agrees that the ignorance is wilful. John Gill multiplies its objects: they know not God, nor themselves, being called gods and forgetting they are men, nor their duty.

On the foundations out of course Adam Clarke reads a political maxim: all the civil institutions of the land totter, since justice stands at the head of all the institutions of a well regulated state, and when it is poisoned every evil must prevail and even religion ceases to have influence. He then breaks off into a comparison with his own country, calling England happy and its judges learned, righteous and impartial, and declaring that never did greater men in their profession dignify any land — a remark he takes care to date. Charles Ellicott hears the same alarm without the consolation: the perversion of judgment strikes the poet as a sign of total anarchy and a dissolution of society, a convulsion like an earthquake, and the very existence of society is threatened when the source of justice is corrupt; he quotes the chorus in which the sacred rivers flow backwards to their source and right and all things veer around their course. John Wesley traces the corruption downward, from the supreme rulers to their inferior officers. Charles Ellicott also marks a pause before this verse, the interval between warning and judgment which is God’s pity and man’s opportunity, and notes that the expostulation falls dead without a response.
6:
In what sense the judges are gods is settled by appeal to their commission. John Gill says they were so by God’s appointment, and reports that our Lord interprets the words of those to whom the word of God came — or rather, he suggests, against whom it came, pronouncing on them the sentence of death; he notes that the Targum reads instead that they are accounted as angels, and that one commentator takes it of angels, though magistrates are undoubtedly meant. Adam Clarke would add the particle of similitude and read like God: they are his representatives, clothed with his power and authority. Matthew Henry points to the statute against treasonable words, in which God himself gives them the style, and asks who can dispute a title from the fountain of honour. John Wesley extends it beyond Israel, to the rulers of all other nations. Charles Ellicott hears the divine voice breaking the silence with an emphatic I: from me comes your office and your honoured title, and now from me hear your doom.

Charles Ellicott adds two afterlives of the verse. It was quoted by the emperor at the opening of the first general council, to remind the bishops that their high office should raise them above jealousy and party feeling; and it gained a further interest from our Lord’s use of it to rebut the charge of blasphemy. On the doom itself he would render the second clause as, altogether will ye princes perish. Adam Clarke presses the comparison harder: they shall die like Adam, who fell from his high perfection and dignity as they have done, their office securing them no immortality; and the falling like one of the princes means they shall not in the course of nature fall into the grave but shall be brought to an end by a legal sentence or a particular judgment. John Gill makes death the leveller, the wise man dying as the fool and the king as the peasant, and adds an eternal death for those who die in their sins. John Wesley renders it only, like ordinary men.

Whom the closing prayer is against divides the two who take it up. Charles Ellicott holds that here at least, if not throughout, the affliction of the community and the perversion of justice by foreign rulers are the motives of the song, and pictures the poet, despairing of the amendment of the corrupt magistrates, taking his case out of their hands as a figure in the play takes his out of the hands of the council, and entrusting it to the Judge of the world. Keil and Delitzsch call that inference erroneous. All peoples are God’s inheritance, and he is asked to maintain his right judicially; but Israel itself, so far as it acts inconsistently with its theocratic character, belies its sanctified nationality and is a nation like the nations, put into the same category with them. Adam Clarke takes the verse forward rather than back, asking whether it does not contain a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles and the prevalence of Christianity, as several of the fathers understood it, and answering that it is only by that universal spread that the reign of righteousness is to be established, and that of no one else can it be said that he shall inherit all nations. John Gill makes it the prayer of the church addressing Christ, that seeing such a corruption in the world he would arise and show himself strong.
